lesson.title: Same Resistor, Different Frequency: Why AC Resistance Is Not Always DC Resistance
lesson.summary: AC resistance is the real, energy-dissipating part of a circuit's impedance; for an ideal resistor it equals the DC value exactly, but real conductors carrying high-frequency current show a higher effective resistance because of the skin effect.
lesson.body:
Ordinary DC resistance describes how a material converts electrical energy into heat: R = rho*L/A for a uniform conductor, and Ohm's law V = IR holds with voltage and current perfectly in step. That same energy-dissipating behavior does not vanish once a circuit runs on alternating current, it simply becomes one piece of a larger picture. In an AC circuit's impedance, Z = R + jX, the R is exactly this real, dissipative resistance, the part of the opposition that stays in phase with current and actually consumes power as heat. The imaginary part X, by contrast, stores energy in a magnetic or electric field for part of the cycle and gives it back later, dissipating nothing on average.

For an idealized resistor, this AC resistance equals the DC resistance at any frequency, full stop. Real wires and components are not quite so obliging. As frequency rises, a changing current inside a conductor generates a changing magnetic field that induces eddy currents opposing the flow of charge near the conductor's center. The net effect, called the skin effect, crowds current toward the outer surface of the conductor, shrinking the effective cross-sectional area it flows through and raising the effective AC resistance above the DC value. The standard measure of how deep current penetrates is the skin depth, delta = sqrt(rho/(pi*f*mu)), the depth at which current density has fallen to about 37 percent, 1/e, of its value at the surface.

Take a round copper wire, resistivity rho = 1.68e-8 ohm meters, permeability essentially mu0 = 4*pi*1e-7 H/m since copper is non-magnetic. At household power frequency, f = 60 Hz, the skin depth is delta = sqrt(1.68e-8 / (pi times 60 times 4*pi*1e-7)), which works out to about 8.42 mm. Now push the frequency up to 1 MHz, typical of radio circuits: delta = sqrt(1.68e-8 / (pi times 1e6 times 4*pi*1e-7)), which works out to about 65.2 micrometers, over a hundred times shallower.

That contrast explains a rule of thumb used throughout basic AC circuit analysis. Ordinary household and low-frequency wiring has a conductor radius well under 8.4 mm, smaller than the 60 Hz skin depth, so current still uses nearly the full cross-section and AC resistance is essentially equal to DC resistance, which is exactly why the impedance triangle you are about to meet simply uses R without a frequency correction. At radio frequencies, though, a skin depth of tens of micrometers means current is confined to a thin shell near the surface, so the effective resistance rises sharply, sometimes by a large factor over the DC value. That is why RF engineers reach for litz wire, many thin insulated strands woven together, or hollow tubing, rather than solid round wire, deliberately maximizing surface area instead of relying on a large solid cross-section that the current would barely use anyway.
